Criterion 2 (1.25 Marks): Implementation of a comprehensive PostgreSQL healthcheck using 'pg_isready' inside the database service definition.
Criterion 3 (1.25 Marks): Updating the backend service dependency to 'depends_on: db: condition: service_healthy'.
Criterion 4 (1.25 Marks): Implementation of application-level retry/backoff connection logic in the backend codebase as an architectural defense-in-depth.

topics.title: CONTINUOUS DELIVERY VS CONTINUOUS DEPLOYMENT
topics.sub: Manual Production Approval Gate vs Automated Direct Release
topics.plain: Continuous Delivery automates testing and packaging so code is always ready to release, but requires human approval. Continuous Deployment pushes every passing commit straight to production.
topics.def: Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment represent the progressive maturity stages of the deployment pipeline: 1. Continuous Delivery (CDe): An automated release engineering discipline where every verified commit automatically builds release artifacts and deploys to staging environments, ensuring code is in a perpetually deployable state; final release to live production requires an explicit manual business approval gate. 2. Continuous Deployment (CDp): The elimination of human approval gates; every single commit that passes the automated CI/CD test and compliance pipeline is automatically and immediately deployed directly into production with zero human intervention.
topics.exam: Continuous Delivery = Automated pipeline with MANUAL button click for production release. Continuous Deployment = 100% automated straight to production with 0 human gates.
topics.trap: Exam Trap: Confusing Continuous Delivery with Continuous Deployment in exams! Continuous Delivery ALWAYS retains a manual business authorization gate for production.
topics.example: A fintech banking platform uses Continuous Delivery to deploy to UAT daily while holding production releases for compliance sign-off; a SaaS startup uses Continuous Deployment to deploy 20 times a day.
topics.q: What is the single operational boundary that distinguishes Continuous Delivery from Continuous Deployment?
topics.a: Continuous Delivery requires an explicit manual human approval gate before releasing to production, whereas Continuous Deployment deploys every passing commit to production fully automatically.

topics.title: BLUE-GREEN DEPLOYMENT STRATEGY
topics.sub: Twin Identical Production Environments & Zero-Downtime Router Switching
topics.plain: Blue-Green runs two identical production setups. Blue serves live users while you deploy new code to Green. Once tested, the router instantly points users to Green with zero downtime.
topics.def: Blue-Green Deployment is a release management strategy that achieves zero downtime and near-instantaneous rollback by provisioning two physically identical production environments: 'Blue' (the currently active live environment serving production traffic) and 'Green' (the idle staging environment). When releasing a new version, engineers deploy and validate artifacts entirely within the idle Green environment. Once smoke tests pass, the upstream router, load balancer, or reverse proxy is toggled to switch 100% of user traffic to Green. If regressions occur, the router immediately switches traffic back to Blue.
topics.exam: Blue = Live active environment. Green = Idle staging environment. Router switches 100% traffic instantly. Rollback = Switch router back to Blue.
topics.trap: Exam Trap: Blue-Green requires stateful database synchronization! Database schema updates must be backward-compatible with both Blue and Green application versions simultaneously.
topics.example: An AWS Route 53 DNS or Application Load Balancer target group switches traffic from Blue EC2 instances to Green EC2 instances in under 1 second.
topics.q: How does Blue-Green deployment achieve near-instantaneous rollback if critical defects emerge after release?
topics.a: Because the old environment ('Blue') remains fully deployed and running idle, rolling back simply requires switching the load balancer router back to the original environment.

topics.title: CANARY RELEASES & TRAFFIC SHIFTING
topics.sub: Progressive Percentage Traffic Slicing & Blast Radius Reduction
topics.plain: A Canary release rolls out changes to a tiny percentage of users (like 5%). If metrics and error rates look good, traffic is slowly increased to 100%, limiting blast radius.
topics.def: A Canary Release is a progressive deployment technique that reduces production risk by routing live user traffic to a new software version in small, incremental percentages. Originating from miners using canaries to detect toxic gas, the deployment routes a tiny fraction of real production traffic (e.g., 2% to 5%) to the 'canary' instances while 95% of users remain on the stable baseline version. Telemetry systems monitor error rates, latency, and system health; if metrics remain within acceptable SLO thresholds, traffic shifts progressively (25%, 50%, 100%); otherwise, traffic is instantly rolled back.
topics.exam: Canary Strategy: Slices traffic progressively (e.g., 5% -> 25% -> 100%). Limits blast radius of bugs. Monitored via real-time telemetry metrics.
topics.trap: Exam Trap: A Canary deployment requires advanced traffic-splitting load balancers or service meshes (like Istio, Envoy, or AWS ALB) to manage weighted traffic routing.
topics.example: Deploying a new recommendation model to 5% of mobile users while monitoring crash logs; detecting an unhandled exception and reverting traffic without affecting 95% of users.
topics.q: What is the primary benefit of deploying a software release using the Canary deployment strategy?
topics.a: It minimizes the blast radius of potential bugs by exposing the new release to only a small fraction of live traffic while monitoring telemetry metrics before global rollout.

topics.title: ROLLING UPDATES & RECREATE STRATEGY
topics.sub: Incremental Pod Replacement, Zero-Downtime vs Temporary Version Skew
topics.plain: Rolling updates replace old pods with new ones gradually, keeping the service online without extra hardware. Recreate kills all old pods before starting new ones, causing downtime.
topics.def: A Rolling Update incrementally replaces instances of an older application version with new instances without downtime. In Kubernetes, the Deployment controller governs this using 'maxSurge' (the maximum number of Pods created above desired replica count) and 'maxUnavailable' (the maximum number of Pods that can be unavailable during update). In contrast, the 'Recreate' strategy terminates all existing application instances simultaneously before spinning up the new version, causing unavoidable service downtime but eliminating temporary version skew.
topics.exam: Rolling Update: Zero downtime, gradual pod replacement, handles version skew. Recreate: Complete downtime, kills all old pods before creating new ones.
topics.trap: Exam Trap: During a rolling update, both old and new versions run concurrently in production for several minutes. All shared database schemas must maintain backward compatibility!
topics.example: A Kubernetes deployment updating 10 replicas with maxUnavailable: 1 and maxSurge: 2, keeping 9 pods running at all times throughout the rollout.
topics.q: What operational challenge must engineers address when using Rolling Updates where multiple application versions run simultaneously in production?
topics.a: Version skew. Database schemas and shared caches must be backward and forward compatible to support concurrent requests handled by both old and new application versions.

topics.title: INFRASTRUCTURE AS CODE (IAC)
topics.sub: Declarative vs Imperative IaC, Idempotency & Drift Detection
topics.plain: IaC defines servers, networks, and cloud resources in code. Declarative IaC states WHAT you want; Imperative IaC states HOW to build it step-by-step. Idempotency ensures consistency.
topics.def: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) is the management, provisioning, and configuration of computing infrastructure (networks, virtual machines, load balancers, database instances) through machine-readable definition files rather than manual physical hardware configuration or interactive configuration tools. IaC is governed by two core paradigms: 1. Declarative IaC (e.g., Terraform, CloudFormation): Specifies the desired end-state ('I want 3 EC2 instances'); the engine computes the execution diff. 2. Imperative IaC (e.g., Bash, AWS CLI): Specifies the step-by-step instructions ('Create instance 1, wait, create instance 2'). Core tenets include Idempotency and Drift Detection.
topics.exam: Declarative = WHAT desired state to achieve (Terraform). Imperative = HOW step-by-step commands to run. Idempotency = Multiple runs produce the EXACT SAME state.
topics.trap: Exam Trap: Configuration Drift occurs when engineers manually modify cloud resources via the web console, desynchronizing real-world infrastructure from IaC code.
topics.example: Running 'terraform apply' to provision an AWS VPC, subnets, and RDS cluster repeatedly without generating duplicate resources due to idempotency.
topics.q: What is meant by the principle of 'Idempotency' in Infrastructure as Code automation?
topics.a: Idempotency guarantees that executing the infrastructure automation script multiple times under identical inputs results in the exact same system state without unintended side effects.

topics.title: TERRAFORM WORKFLOW & ARCHITECTURE
topics.sub: State File Management, Providers, plan, apply & HCL Declarations
topics.plain: Terraform provisions cloud resources using HashiCorp Configuration Language (HCL). The core workflow is init -> plan (preview changes) -> apply (provision resources).
topics.def: Terraform is an open-source declarative Infrastructure as Code tool created by HashiCorp. It utilizes HashiCorp Configuration Language (HCL) and modular cloud 'Providers' (AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes) to manage infrastructure lifecycles. The core CLI workflow comprises: 1. 'terraform init' (downloads required provider plugins), 2. 'terraform plan' (compares declared code against real-world state, emitting an execution plan diff), 3. 'terraform apply' (provisions infrastructure), and 4. 'terraform destroy' (tears down resources). The 'terraform.tfstate' file maps declared configuration resources to real-world cloud IDs.
topics.exam: Workflow: init -> plan -> apply -> destroy. State File (terraform.tfstate): Maps declared code to real-world resource IDs. Must be locked remotely in S3/DynamoDB.
topics.trap: Exam Trap: Storing terraform.tfstate locally in team projects causes race conditions and state corruption! Always use remote backends with state locking (e.g., S3 + DynamoDB).
topics.example: A Terraform block 'resource "aws_s3_bucket" "logs" { bucket = "my-audit-logs" }' provisions an S3 bucket when 'terraform apply' is executed.
topics.q: What is the critical function of the 'terraform.tfstate' state file in HashiCorp Terraform?
topics.a: It records the metadata mapping of your declared HCL configuration to real-world cloud resource IDs and attributes, enabling Terraform to calculate changes and detect drift.

topics.title: ANSIBLE CONFIGURATION MANAGEMENT
topics.sub: Agentless Architecture, SSH Transport, YAML Playbooks & Idempotency
topics.plain: Ansible automates server configuration over SSH without installing any background agents. Playbooks are written in YAML, declaring tasks executed by idempotent modules.
topics.def: Ansible is an open-source automation engine for configuration management, application deployment, and intra-service orchestration. Key architectural characteristics include: 1. Agentless Architecture: Requires no background software daemons installed on managed target nodes; communicates entirely over standard OpenSSH (Linux) or WinRM (Windows) and Python. 2. Inventory: An INI or YAML file defining host IPs and group classifications. 3. Playbooks: Declarative YAML files mapping host groups to tasks. 4. Modules: Discrete units of idempotent execution (e.g., 'apt', 'yum', 'copy', 'service', 'user') that ensure changes are only made if current state does not match desired state.
topics.exam: Ansible = Agentless (uses SSH, zero daemon overhead). YAML Playbooks. Idempotent modules (only applies changes if current state differs).
topics.trap: Exam Trap: Using the raw 'command' or 'shell' module in Ansible bypasses idempotency! Always use specialized modules like 'apt' or 'file' that guarantee idempotent execution.
topics.example: An Ansible playbook that installs Nginx on 50 web servers, copies custom nginx.conf, and ensures the systemd service is active and enabled on boot.
topics.q: Why is Ansible referred to as an 'Agentless' configuration management system?
topics.a: Because it does not require installing or maintaining proprietary background client daemon software on target managed nodes; it operates entirely over standard SSH and Python.

topics.title: THE THREE PILLARS OF OBSERVABILITY
topics.sub: Metrics, Centralized Logs, Distributed Tracing & High Cardinality
topics.plain: Observability lets you understand system internals by looking at external outputs: Metrics (what is happening over time), Logs (why it happened), and Traces (where latency occurred).
topics.def: Observability is a measure of how well internal states of a distributed software system can be inferred solely from knowledge of its external telemetry outputs. It is established on Three Pillars: 1. Metrics: Numerically aggregated, timestamped quantitative values measured over intervals (e.g., CPU utilization, memory consumption, request throughput, error rate) optimized for real-time alerting. 2. Logs: Structured, timestamped, immutable event records providing deep forensic narrative context (e.g., stack traces, SQL syntax errors, authentication failures). 3. Distributed Traces: End-to-end request lifecycle paths tracked across microservices using unique Trace IDs and Span IDs to diagnose latency bottlenecks.
topics.exam: Three Pillars: Metrics (Aggregated numbers: PromQL, CPU%), Logs (Detailed event records: ELK, stack traces), Traces (Request journey across microservices: Jaeger).
topics.trap: Exam Trap: Monitoring tells you WHEN a system is broken (dashboard turns red); Observability allows you to query and understand WHY unexpected failures occurred.
topics.example: A Prometheus alert flags high HTTP 500 error rate (Metric), Elasticsearch pinpoints an unhandled NullPointerException (Log), and Jaeger isolates a 3-second database lock (Trace).
topics.q: In distributed systems observability, what is the specific role of Distributed Tracing compared to metrics and logs?
topics.a: Distributed Tracing tracks the end-to-end execution path of a user request as it traverses across multiple microservices, identifying exact latency bottlenecks and failing hops.

topics.title: PROMETHEUS METRIC MONITORING
topics.sub: Pull-Based HTTP Scraping, TSDB, Exporters & PromQL
topics.plain: Prometheus is a time-series monitoring system. It scrapes numerical metrics over HTTP from targets at regular intervals, stores them in a TSDB, and queries them with PromQL.
topics.def: Prometheus is an open-source systems monitoring and alerting toolkit graduated by the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF). Architecture features: 1. Pull-Based Model: The Prometheus server periodically scrapes HTTP endpoints (typically '/metrics') exposed by target services or specialized 'Exporters' (e.g., Node Exporter, Blackbox Exporter). 2. Time Series Database (TSDB): Stores multi-dimensional data identified by metric name and key-value label pairs. 3. Four Metric Types: Counter (monotonically increasing value, e.g., total requests), Gauge (value that fluctuates up and down, e.g., memory usage), Histogram, and Summary. 4. PromQL: Powerful functional query language.
topics.exam: Prometheus Architecture: Pull-based scraping (HTTP GET /metrics). TSDB storage. Metric Types: Counter (only goes up), Gauge (goes up and down). Query: PromQL.
topics.trap: Exam Trap: Do NOT use a Prometheus Counter to measure fluctuating values like free disk space or active connections! Always use a Gauge for values that rise and fall.
topics.example: A PromQL query 'rate(http_requests_total{status=~'5..'}[5m]) > 0.05' triggers Alertmanager when the 5-minute HTTP 5xx error rate exceeds 5%.
topics.q: What is the primary difference between a Prometheus 'Counter' and 'Gauge' metric type?
topics.a: A Counter can only increment monotonically (or reset to zero on restart), whereas a Gauge represents a value that can arbitrarily increase and decrease over time.

topics.title: GRAFANA OBSERVABILITY DASHBOARDS
topics.sub: Data Source Integrations, Threshold Alerting & Visual Operations
topics.plain: Grafana is an analytics and visualization platform. It connects to multiple data sources (Prometheus, Loki, Elasticsearch) to render real-time interactive operations dashboards.
topics.def: Grafana is an open-source operational visualization, analytics, and multi-platform dashboarding platform. Rather than storing data, Grafana connects to disparate heterogeneous data sources (Prometheus for time-series metrics, Loki for logs, Tempo for traces, PostgreSQL, AWS CloudWatch) through pluggable data source integrations. It translates backend queries (like PromQL or LogQL) into customizable panels (heatmaps, time-series graphs, single-stat gauges, geoloaction maps). Grafana supports dynamic templating variables, annotations for deployment markers, and unified threshold-based multi-channel alert routing.
topics.exam: Grafana = Visualization and dashboarding layer. Connects to Prometheus, Loki, Elasticsearch. Does NOT store telemetry data itself.
topics.trap: Exam Trap: Grafana is not a metric storage database! It is purely a visualization frontend that queries underlying data engines like Prometheus or Elasticsearch.
topics.example: An SRE operational dashboard in Grafana showing 99th percentile request latency, Kubernetes pod CPU saturation, and deployment release annotations side-by-side.
topics.q: What role does Grafana play in a modern DevOps observability stack alongside Prometheus and Loki?
topics.a: Grafana serves as the centralized visualization and dashboarding engine, querying underlying time-series databases and log engines without storing the telemetry data itself.

topics.title: CENTRALIZED LOG AGGREGATION
topics.sub: ELK Stack, Fluentd, Loki, Structured JSON Logging & Log Rotation
topics.plain: Centralized logging aggregates logs from hundreds of servers into one searchable index (Elasticsearch/Loki), using shippers like Fluentd/Logstash and searching via Kibana.
topics.def: Centralized Log Aggregation solves the operational limitation of ephemeral container logging by shipping, parsing, indexing, and storing log outputs across distributed systems into a single searchable data lake. Standard architectures include: 1. The ELK / EFK Stack: Elasticsearch (distributed search and indexing engine), Logstash or Fluentd/Fluent Bit (log shipper, parser, and transformer), and Kibana (search and visualization UI). 2. Grafana Loki: A modern, cost-effective Prometheus-inspired log aggregation system that indexes only metadata labels rather than full text, slashing storage and RAM footprint requirements.
topics.exam: ELK Stack: Elasticsearch (Index/Search), Logstash/Fluentd (Shipper/Parser), Kibana (Visualization). Loki: Lightweight log aggregation indexed by labels.
topics.trap: Exam Trap: Logging raw unstructured text strings makes programmatic parsing impossible in high-volume microservices; always emit structured JSON logs with correlation IDs.
topics.example: A microservice writes JSON logs to stdout; Fluent Bit ships them to Elasticsearch, allowing engineers to query 'error_code: 503 AND customer_id: 1042' in Kibana.
topics.q: Why do modern cloud-native architectures favor structured JSON logging over raw plain-text string logging in application containers?
topics.a: Structured JSON logs can be automatically parsed, indexed, and filtered by log aggregation engines (like Elasticsearch or Loki) using discrete key-value fields without brittle regex parsing.

topics.title: HEALTH PROBES & AUTOMATED ROLLBACKS
topics.sub: Liveness vs Readiness Probes, /healthz & Automated Circuit Breaking
topics.plain: Liveness probes restart a frozen container. Readiness probes take a busy container out of the load balancer. If an update fails, automated rollbacks revert instantly.
topics.def: Container reliability and automated failure recovery are governed by health probes and automated rollback controllers: 1. Liveness Probe: Verifies whether the container process is still alive and functioning; if the probe fails (e.g., deadlock occurs), the orchestrator immediately kills and restarts the container. 2. Readiness Probe: Verifies whether the container is ready to accept incoming user traffic; if it fails (e.g., warming up caches), the container's IP is temporarily removed from service load balancing endpoints without restarting the pod. Automated rollbacks monitor probe success and deployment error thresholds, automatically issuing rollbacks if errors spike.
topics.exam: Liveness = Is process healthy? (Fail -> RESTART container). Readiness = Can it accept traffic? (Fail -> REMOVE from load balancer endpoints, DO NOT restart).
topics.trap: Exam Trap: Making a Liveness probe check external dependencies (like an external database) is a critical anti-pattern! If the database slows down, all your containers will restart in a cascading crash loop!
topics.example: Configuring 'httpGet: path: /healthz, port: 8080' with 'failureThreshold: 3' in a Kubernetes pod specification to safeguard against memory deadlocks.
topics.q: What happens when a Kubernetes container fails its configured Readiness Probe versus when it fails its Liveness Probe?
topics.a: Failing a Readiness Probe temporarily removes the Pod from Service load balancer traffic without restarting it; failing a Liveness Probe causes the kubelet to restart the container.

quiz.q: What is the defining operational distinction between Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment?
opts: Continuous Delivery is only compatible with bare-metal servers, while Continuous Deployment requires serverless cloud functions
Continuous Delivery requires a manual human authorization gate before production release; Continuous Deployment releases automatically without manual gates
Continuous Delivery does not require automated testing, while Continuous Deployment relies on manual spreadsheet checks
Continuous Delivery only compiles code once per week, while Continuous Deployment compiles code continuously
quiz.correctFb: In Continuous Delivery, every passing build produces deployable artifacts, but promotion to live production requires manual approval. Continuous Deployment automates production deployment directly.
distractors: Both delivery and deployment can target bare-metal servers, virtual machines, containers, or serverless infrastructure.
Both methodologies strictly require automated testing; Continuous Delivery cannot function without automated verification.
Both models compile and verify code continuously upon commit.

quiz.q: In a Blue-Green deployment strategy, how does an engineering team execute an immediate rollback if the newly released Green environment exhibits critical bugs?
opts: By switching the load balancer or router traffic back to the still-running Blue environment
By recompiling the entire application from scratch on production servers
By manually re-installing the operating system on all physical host machines
By restoring the entire hard drive from offline physical tape storage
quiz.correctFb: Because the Blue environment remains active and fully intact while Green handles initial live traffic, rolling back is instantaneous by toggling the router back to Blue.
distractors: Recompiling from scratch takes significant time and violates zero-downtime, immutable artifact deployment principles.
Re-installing the operating system is a destructive disaster recovery action, not a deployment rollback mechanism.
Tape storage restorations require hours or days and are reserved for catastrophic disaster recovery.

quiz.q: What is the primary advantage of employing a Canary Release deployment strategy?
opts: It cuts cloud computing infrastructure costs to zero dollars
It automatically fixes all syntax errors in Python and Java source code
It eliminates the need for unit testing and code linting during development
It routes a small percentage (e.g., 5%) of live traffic to the new version, limiting the blast radius of unexpected defects
quiz.correctFb: Canary releases limit the blast radius by exposing new features to a small slice of real users, monitoring error rates and latency before expanding rollout.
distractors: Deployment strategies do not fix application syntax errors; that is the responsibility of compilers and linters in CI.
Canary deployments require robust automated testing; they are not a substitute for unit or integration tests.
Canary deployments require running multiple concurrent environments, slightly increasing compute costs rather than reducing them to zero.

quiz.q: What critical operational challenge arises during a Rolling Update when both old and new application instances run simultaneously in production?
opts: All user passwords must be reset across the entire user base
The server's physical CPU cores permanently lose half their clock speed
Version skew, requiring shared database schemas and API contracts to remain backward and forward compatible
Docker Engine automatically deletes all container images from disk
quiz.correctFb: Version skew occurs during rolling updates because requests hit old and new versions concurrently. Shared databases and caches must maintain two-way compatibility.
distractors: Rolling updates do not alter physical CPU hardware clock frequencies.
Rolling updates do not necessitate user password resets.
Docker Engine does not delete images during active rolling updates.

quiz.q: Which Infrastructure as Code characteristic guarantees that executing an automation script multiple times produces the exact same end-state without duplicate resources?
opts: Polymorphism
Idempotency
Concurrency
Encapsulation
quiz.correctFb: Idempotency ensures that no matter how many times an IaC configuration is executed, the resulting infrastructure state matches the declared specification exactly without side effects.
distractors: Polymorphism is an object-oriented programming concept allowing objects to take multiple forms.
Concurrency relates to executing multiple computations simultaneously, not consistency of state outcomes.
Encapsulation is an OOP principle restricting direct access to object components.

quiz.q: Which command in the HashiCorp Terraform workflow generates an execution diff showing exactly what cloud resources will be created, modified, or destroyed?
opts: terraform plan
terraform init
terraform apply
terraform fmt
quiz.correctFb: 'terraform plan' compares declared HCL files against the state file and live cloud environment, outputting a precise execution plan diff of proposed actions.
distractors: 'terraform init' initializes the working directory by downloading provider plugins and configuring backends.
'terraform apply' actually executes the actions to provision or modify real-world infrastructure.
'terraform fmt' rewrites Terraform configuration files into a canonical format and style.

quiz.q: Why is Ansible categorized as an 'Agentless' configuration management tool?
opts: It runs exclusively on Windows 98 operating systems
It does not require developers to write code or configuration files
It can only manage physical hardware routers and switches, not servers
It connects to managed nodes over standard SSH without requiring background daemon software installed on targets
quiz.correctFb: Ansible operates over OpenSSH or WinRM to execute tasks using native Python on the target host, eliminating the overhead of managing agent software.
distractors: Ansible requires writing structured YAML playbooks and configuration files.
Ansible manages Linux and Windows servers, cloud instances, and containers, not just hardware switches.
Ansible runs on modern UNIX-like operating systems (Linux, macOS) and manages modern infrastructure.

quiz.q: Which of the following represents the Three Pillars of Observability in modern distributed software engineering?
opts: CPU, Memory, and Disk Storage
HTML, CSS, and JavaScript
Metrics, Logs, and Distributed Traces
Monolithic, Microservices, and Serverless
quiz.correctFb: The Three Pillars of Observability are Metrics (aggregated time-series numbers), Logs (timestamped event records), and Distributed Traces (end-to-end request journeys).
distractors: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript are web frontend presentation and scripting technologies.
CPU, Memory, and Disk are physical hardware compute resources, not observability telemetry pillars.
Monolithic, Microservices, and Serverless are architectural software design patterns.

quiz.q: What metric collection architecture does Prometheus use to gather numerical time-series data from monitored applications and exporters?
opts: Push-based model where clients stream UDP packets continuously to Prometheus
Pull-based model via HTTP scraping of '/metrics' endpoints
Polling database tables via raw SQL queries every 24 hours
Reading physical paper printer logs using optical character recognition
quiz.correctFb: Prometheus uses a pull-based model: the server periodically initiates an HTTP GET request to scrape '/metrics' endpoints hosted by target applications and exporters.
distractors: Push-based streaming over UDP is characteristic of tools like StatsD, not core Prometheus server architecture.
Prometheus scrapes time-series data at high frequencies (seconds) over HTTP, not via daily SQL queries.
Optical character recognition on paper logs is absurd in digital cloud observability.

quiz.q: In Kubernetes, what action does the kubelet perform when an application container fails its configured Liveness Probe?
opts: It terminates and restarts the failed container process according to its restartPolicy
It temporarily removes the Pod from Service load balancer traffic without restarting it
It immediately deletes the entire Kubernetes cluster control plane
It sends an automated SMS message to all cluster administrators
quiz.correctFb: Liveness probes detect deadlocks or unrecoverable process states. When a Liveness probe fails, kubelet terminates and restarts the container to restore health.
distractors: Temporarily removing the Pod from service load balancer traffic without restarting is the exact behavior of a failed Readiness Probe.
Failing a container probe never damages or deletes the cluster control plane.
Kubelet does not send SMS messages; alert routing is handled by external tools like Alertmanager.

quiz.q: Why is Grafana commonly deployed alongside Prometheus in enterprise DevOps monitoring stacks?
opts: Grafana acts as an anti-virus scanner for Docker container images
Grafana is required to store time-series metrics because Prometheus cannot store data
Grafana compiles Prometheus C++ source code into binary executables
Grafana provides a flexible, interactive dashboarding and visualization layer that queries Prometheus time-series data
quiz.correctFb: Grafana provides dynamic visualization, querying Prometheus via PromQL and rendering real-time graphs, charts, and alert panels.
distractors: Prometheus includes its own built-in time-series database (TSDB); Grafana does not store metrics.
Prometheus is written in Go and does not require Grafana for compilation.
Grafana is a dashboarding platform, not an anti-virus or image vulnerability scanner.

bossChallenges.scenario: [10 MARKS] University Exam Question: Contrast Continuous Delivery versus Continuous Deployment, and analyze the four modern deployment strategies (Recreate, Rolling Update, Blue-Green, and Canary). Evaluate each strategy across downtime impact, hardware resource overhead, rollback complexity, and version skew management. Conclude with a comprehensive Terraform and Prometheus architecture ensuring automated rollbacks upon SLO violation.
rubric: Criterion 1 (2.5 Marks): Precise differentiation between Continuous Delivery (human approval gate) and Continuous Deployment (100% automated release).
Criterion 2 (2.5 Marks): Comparative matrix evaluating Recreate, Rolling, Blue-Green, and Canary across downtime, cost, rollback, and version skew.
Criterion 3 (2.5 Marks): Technical breakdown of Infrastructure as Code (IaC) principles: Idempotency, Declarative HCL, and State locking.
Criterion 4 (2.5 Marks): End-to-end telemetry architecture linking Prometheus metric scraping, PromQL alert rules, and automated orchestrator rollback hooks.

bossChallenges.scenario: [5 MARKS] Practical Problem-Solving Scenario: A junior developer configured a Kubernetes Liveness Probe to query an external shared MySQL database: 'httpGet: path: /health/db'. During peak traffic, the database experienced query latency spikes, causing the Liveness Probe to time out across all 20 API pods simultaneously. All 20 pods crashed into an endless restart loop, taking down the entire web platform. Diagnose the architectural anti-pattern and provide the correct health probe design.
rubric: Criterion 1 (1.25 Marks): Diagnosis identifying the cascading failure anti-pattern: tying a local Liveness probe to a shared downstream external dependency.
Criterion 2 (1.25 Marks): Architectural separation of Liveness Probes (pure internal process health checking, e.g. memory deadlock / event loop responsiveness).
Criterion 3 (1.25 Marks): Proper utilization of Readiness Probes to decouple traffic routing from process restarts during external database saturation.
Criterion 4 (1.25 Marks): Implementation of circuit breakers, connection pools, and graceful HTTP /healthz and /readyz probe endpoints.
